trendNotes.label: Group 14
trendNotes.essay: Descending from Carbon (C) to Silicon (Si) exhibits the classic inner-core shielding effect. The additional 3s²3p² shell increases the atomic radius significantly (+58%), causing valence electrons to experience a diminished effective nuclear charge (Z_eff). C–C bonds drastically outlast weaker Si–Si bonds. Silicon's network is an intrinsic semiconductor.

trendNotes.label: Group 17
trendNotes.essay: Fluorine to chlorine is the textbook halogen step: both want one electron, but fluorine is a much fiercer oxidizer because it is smaller and more electronegative. Chlorine still disinfects and forms a wide oxo-anion ladder (ClO⁻ to ClO₄⁻) that fluorine barely copies.

trendNotes.label: Group 1
trendNotes.essay: Lithium to sodium keeps the ns¹ pattern, but sodium’s extra shell makes the atom larger and easier to oxidize. Lithium’s small Li⁺ ion polarizes anions and dominates battery electrochemistry; sodium remains the everyday salt cation.

trendNotes.label: Group 18
trendNotes.essay: Neon and argon are both closed-shell gases, but argon is denser and far more abundant in air. Neither forms ordinary molecules; argon’s chemistry, like krypton’s, is a specialist topic, while neon is the lighting benchmark.

discovery.text: Isolated as inflammable air; later named hydrogen by Lavoisier.

elements.history:
In 1766 Henry Cavendish collected a gas from metals and acids and called it inflammable air. He showed that burning it produced water. Antoine Lavoisier later named it hydrogen, from the Greek for water-former, and listed it as an element.

The common isotope, protium, is a single proton. Deuterium was identified in 1931 and tritium in 1934. In 1913 the Balmer lines of hydrogen became the first spectrum explained by Bohr’s model of the atom.
elements.howDiscovered:
Henry Cavendish collected a gas by pouring acid onto iron, zinc, and tin and catching what bubbled off. The gas burned. In 1781 he exploded measured amounts of it with air and found that the product was water, and that the gas’s weight accounted for the water’s weight.

That closed the argument that the gas was a modification of ordinary air. Antoine Lavoisier repeated the combination, named the gas hydrogen, and put it on his list of elements. The discovery was a weighed reaction, not a new mineral.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Almost every hydrogen nucleus was made in the first few minutes of the Universe, once it had cooled enough for protons and neutrons to stick and before it cooled too far for them to fuse. The common isotope, protium, is that leftover proton. Deuterium was made in the same brief window. Stars destroy deuterium, so the deuterium still around is a fossil of those minutes.

Stars burn hydrogen into helium. They do not replace the cosmic supply. Tritium is a different, short-lived nucleus, knocked together by cosmic rays, and it is not part of the primordial stock.

trivia.title: Inflammable Air from Acids
trivia.summary: Henry Cavendish trapped the gas that metals give off in acid and found that it burned. What the flame left behind was the real surprise.
trivia.story: Henry Cavendish preferred a quiet bench and a balance to a crowd. When metals sat in acid, a gas bubbled off, and he caught it instead of letting it drift away. A flame set the gas alight, so he called it inflammable air and measured how it behaved. He then burned a weighed portion and collected the product, expecting some sharp or sooty residue. What he found was water. His account in 1766 made inflammable air a substance in its own right, years before a classroom name was attached to the letter H.

trivia.title: The Name Water-Former
trivia.summary: Antoine Lavoisier wanted chemical names to describe what substances actually did. A burning gas that produced water gave him a chance to prove the point.
trivia.story: Antoine Lavoisier was stripping old language out of chemistry and replacing it with names that reported facts. He knew the inflammable air from the English experiments, and he knew that burning it in oxygen produced water. He built the name hydrogen from Greek words meaning water-former. The name carried a claim: the gas was an element, and water was a compound, not an element itself. On the list of simple substances that he published, hydrogen had a place of its own. Students still write that choice every time they put an H at the start of a formula.

trivia.title: Fire at the Landing Field
trivia.summary: A famous passenger airship reached New Jersey in 1937 with a crowd waiting below. The landing turned into a fire before anyone could step safely away.
trivia.story: The Hindenburg had crossed the ocean and was easing toward its mast in New Jersey on a May evening in 1937. People on the field looked up at the huge silver shape. Then flame ran over the covering, and the ship fell in fire and wreckage while the landing crew scattered. For years afterward, investigators debated what made the first spark. They did not debate the lifting gas. The cells had been filled with hydrogen, which burns, because the helium that does not burn had not been made available for that ship.

trivia.title: Heavy Hydrogen in the Residue
trivia.summary: Harold Urey believed ordinary hydrogen hid a heavier twin in tiny amounts. Finding it meant staring at what was left after most of the sample was gone.
trivia.story: Nearly every hydrogen atom is the lightest atom there is, one proton and one electron. Harold Urey was convinced that a heavier stable twin existed and was simply scarce. In 1931 he took liquid hydrogen and let the bulk of it boil away, so that anything heavier would linger in the last fraction. He examined the light from that remainder. Extra lines sat where he had predicted a heavy isotope should announce itself. He named it deuterium, and hydrogen was no longer a single kind of atom but a small family.

trivia.title: A Balloon Ride on Hydrogen
trivia.summary: Soon after hot-air balloons left the ground, Jacques Charles prepared a silk balloon filled with a lighter gas. Paris was about to watch a different kind of flight.
trivia.story: Hot air was not the only way to rise. Jacques Charles filled a silk balloon with hydrogen, the light gas already known to catch fire, and in 1783 he stepped into the basket above Paris. The globe lifted because the gas inside weighed far less than the air it pushed aside. Crowds saw a man travel on a laboratory curiosity. Charles landed famous, and hydrogen had a public use at last. The same lightness that carried him remained a risk, since a flame and a torn bag could undo the triumph in a moment.

discovery.text: Known as charcoal, soot, and diamond long before it was an element.

elements.history:
Charcoal, soot, and diamond were known long before anyone called them one element. In 1772 Lavoisier burned a diamond in oxygen and obtained the same gas as from burning charcoal, which tied the forms together. The name carbon is from the Latin carbo, coal.

The nineteenth century sorted the allotropes. Graphite, diamond, and later fullerenes and graphene are the same element in different networks, and organic chemistry is the chemistry of its chains.
elements.howDiscovered:
Charcoal, soot, and diamond were familiar long before anyone treated them as one element. The experiment that tied them together was combustion. In 1772 Antoine Lavoisier burned a diamond in a closed vessel with a burning glass and collected the same fixed air that burning charcoal produced.

He weighed the vessel. The gas accounted for the diamond. Graphite later joined them. Carbon was discovered by showing that three very different solids were the same simple substance, because each of them became carbon dioxide and nothing else.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Carbon is built in the cores of stars that are burning helium. Three helium nuclei meet and make carbon-12, the triple-alpha step. A little of that carbon captures one more helium nucleus and becomes oxygen, so the amount of carbon a star returns depends on how the race between those two captures goes.

Red giants and massive stars both run the reaction. Winds and supernovae put the carbon into space. The carbon in coal, diamond, and living tissue is that stellar ash, gathered into the cloud that became the solar system.

trivia.title: The Diamond and the Charcoal
trivia.summary: A diamond and a lump of charcoal did not look like relatives. Antoine Lavoisier burned the jewel to see whether the difference survived the fire.
trivia.story: Diamond, charcoal, and soot had lived in different trades for centuries, and almost nobody treated them as one substance. In 1772 Antoine Lavoisier used a powerful burning lens to heat a diamond in oxygen until the stone was gone. He collected the gas that formed. It was the same gas he obtained when charcoal burned. The glittering mineral and the black fuel had been carbon in two disguises. The experiment did not make diamonds cheap, but it ended the idea that a jewel was a private kind of matter with no link to the hearth.

trivia.title: A Name Taken from Coal
trivia.summary: Once diamond and charcoal were the same element, the element needed a word. Latin already had a plain name for coal, and chemistry borrowed it.
trivia.story: Lavoisier's burning diamond showed a kinship, and the kinship needed a label that miners and jewelers could share. The word chosen was carbon, from the Latin carbo, coal. It pointed at the familiar black fuel rather than at the rare crystal. That was a deliberate plainness. Coal, charcoal, and later graphite could all sit under one name even when they looked nothing alike. The name also marked a boundary: carbon was an element, and the endless compounds of life and industry would be built from it rather than confused with it.

trivia.title: Sixty Atoms in a Ball
trivia.summary: Soot from a hot carbon experiment was supposed to be ordinary mess. In 1985 a few researchers found a molecule in it with a shape nobody had planned.
trivia.story: Graphite and diamond were the famous forms, and then a third shape turned up in the soot. In 1985 Harold Kroto, Richard Smalley, and Robert Curl vaporized graphite and found molecules made of sixty carbon atoms. The atoms closed into a hollow ball, a pattern of hexagons and pentagons like a football. They called the molecules buckminsterfullerene, soon nicknamed buckyballs, after the domes of Buckminster Fuller. Carbon, the element of coal and diamonds, could also curl into a cage. The discovery opened a family of forms that older textbooks had no page for.

trivia.title: A Gas with No Warning Smell
trivia.summary: Charcoal and coal have warmed rooms for centuries. The danger in a closed space is not always the flame you can see.
trivia.story: Carbon is the fuel in charcoal and in coal, and a bright fire looks like the whole story. Carbon monoxide, a gas with no color and no useful smell, can come from a fire that does not burn cleanly. People who slept near poorly vented stoves have been poisoned by it. The gas grips the blood in place of oxygen, so a sleeper grows drowsy and may never wake. The hazard is old and ordinary, which is why it keeps returning in winter rooms and in garages. Carbon's cheerful fire and this invisible gas are closer neighbors than the flames suggest.

trivia.title: The Pencil That Was Not Lead
trivia.summary: Writers called the dark core of a pencil lead, and the mineral itself was once sold under a name that meant the same. The mark on the page was never that metal.
trivia.story: A pencil line looks like soft metal rubbed onto paper, and for a long time people said lead because that is what the darkness resembled. The mineral in the stick was graphite, a form of carbon, nicknamed black lead or plumbago. Clay mixed with the graphite made the core harder or softer, which is why pencils come in grades. No lead was required for the mark. The confusion lasted in ordinary speech even after chemists had separated the element from the metal it imitates. Every homework sentence written in pencil is a small deposit of carbon.

discovery.text: Isolated from liquefied air after argon and krypton.

elements.history:
William Ramsay and Morris Travers isolated neon in 1898 by fractional distillation of liquid air, after they had already found argon, krypton, and xenon. A new crimson glow in a discharge tube told them the fraction was a new gas. They named it neon, from the Greek neos, new.

Georges Claude turned that glow into commercial lighting in the 1910s. Neon signs made the element a public word, even when later tubes used other gases for other colors.
elements.howDiscovered:
William Ramsay and Morris Travers liquefied air and distilled it in fractions. After argon had been removed, a light fraction sparked in a discharge tube with a crimson glow that matched no known gas. They collected it in 1898 and named it from the newness of the line.

The amount in air is small, about 18 parts per million, which is why the gas waited until liquid air could be taken apart carefully. The discovery was a boiling point and a spectrum. There was no mineral and no chemical reaction, only a fraction that glowed a color argon did not.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Neon-20, the common isotope, is built by carbon burning in massive stars. Two carbon nuclei fuse, and one frequent result is neon plus a helium nucleus. The supernova that ends the star returns that neon to space.

Neon-22 has a second path. Helium burning on nitrogen-14 builds it in massive stars and in giants, and that neon-22 also releases neutrons those stars use for slow capture of heavier elements. The neon in air is mostly the neon-20 from massive stars.

trivia.title: A Crimson Glow in Cold Air
trivia.summary: William Ramsay and Morris Travers were separating the gases dissolved in liquid air. One fraction, sparked in a tube, shone a color they had not already assigned.
trivia.story: Argon was already known when William Ramsay and Morris Travers started distilling liquid air in earnest. In 1898 they collected fraction after fraction, looking for anything that was not oxygen, nitrogen, or the gases they had already named. A discharge tube was their witness. One fraction glowed a brilliant crimson that matched no familiar fill. The color was the announcement. They had a new element in the cold residue of ordinary air, present in a trace and impossible to see until the rest of the air had been peeled away.

trivia.title: The Gas Named New
trivia.summary: The crimson fraction needed a name that would not pretend the gas had been familiar. Greek supplied a short word for exactly that situation.
trivia.story: Ramsay and Travers did not reach for a mineral or a homeland when they named the new gas. They chose neon, from the Greek neos, meaning new. The word recorded the experience of the experiment: a fraction that had not been on yesterday's list. It was a modest name beside helium's Sun and argon's idleness, and it fit a gas found in scraps. Neon is scarce in air, which is why it had waited until liquid air could be taken apart carefully. The name says discovery, not origin in a mountain or a myth.

trivia.title: Letters Hired the Glow
trivia.summary: The crimson discharge that identified neon was too striking to leave in a physics tube. An inventor turned it into writing that a street could read.
trivia.story: A glow in a laboratory tube is a result. Georges Claude looked at the same glow and saw a sign. In the 1910s he bent glass tubes into letters and filled them so that neon's red-orange light could spell a shop or a product above a sidewalk. The tubes drew current, the gas shone, and advertising acquired a night color of its own. Cities changed after dark. An element isolated by patient distillation became one of the few that ordinary people could point at and name, even if they never learned how small its share of the air is.

trivia.title: When the Sign Is Another Gas
trivia.summary: Nighttime letters in blue, green, or white are often still called neon. The word survived a change that the gas itself did not make.
trivia.story: Claude's first successful signs used neon, and the red light taught the public the element's name. Later tubes needed other colors, and other gases and coatings supplied them. A blue letter might contain a different fill entirely, yet the whole craft kept the name neon. The mismatch is a small public confusion with a real history behind it. Neon remains the classic red-orange, and the word on the street became larger than the element. Ramsay's new gas had donated its name to a kind of light, including lights that no longer needed it.

trivia.title: Almost Lost in the Distillate
trivia.summary: Liquid air holds only a trace of the new gas, and a clumsy fraction would have thrown it away. The crimson tube was what stopped the chemists from moving on.
trivia.story: Neon does not announce itself in a room. There is too little of it in each breath, and it does nothing colorful until electricity is passed through a concentrated sample. Ramsay and Travers could easily have filed the faint fraction with leftovers and gone on to the next boiling point, and the discharge tube made the miss harder. Crimson light is a poor thing to ignore, and they did not ignore it, and the episode is not an accident with a victim. It is a near-miss in a cold laboratory, rescued by a color. The element named new was almost an unnamed residue.

discovery.text: Isolated from silica after earlier work by Gay-Lussac and Thenard.

elements.history:
Silica, as flint, quartz, and glass, is ancient. In 1824 Jöns Jacob Berzelius isolated reasonably pure silicon by reducing potassium fluorosilicate. The name, which he gave, is from the Latin silex, flint. Gay-Lussac and Thénard had prepared an impure form earlier.

Silicon was a chemical footnote until the twentieth century. Zone refining and the transistor turned the element into the semiconductor of electronics, while silica remained the network of glass and rock.
elements.howDiscovered:
Jöns Jacob Berzelius heated potassium metal with potassium fluorosilicate in 1824, washed the mass with water until the soluble salts were gone, and was left with a brown amorphous powder. The powder burned to silica. Gay-Lussac and Thénard had seen a similar impure material earlier and had not established it.

Silica, as flint and quartz, was ancient. The element was the powder that could be burned back to silica and that was not carbon. Berzelius’s washing step is what made the claim convincing: the potassium and the fluoride were gone, and the residue was still there.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Silicon-28 is the principal ash of oxygen burning in massive stars. Oxygen nuclei fuse, and the burning tends toward silicon, the most tightly bound nucleus the star can stockpile before the final collapse. Silicon burning then consumes part of that stock on the way to iron.

What survives is the silicon the explosion freezes before the conversion can finish. Silicon-29 and silicon-30 take a share of neutrons during the same burning. Sand, glass, and the rocky planets are largely this frozen supernova ash.

trivia.title: Named for a Piece of Flint
trivia.summary: Flint, quartz, and glass were ancient crafts before anyone isolated the element in them. The Latin word for flint became the element's name.
trivia.story: People knapped flint into tools, melted sand into glass, and set quartz in jewelry without a theory of elements, and the common ingredient was silica. When Jöns Jacob Berzelius finally had a sample of the element itself, he named it from the Latin silex, flint. Silicon is a scholar's word for a substance the Stone Age had already used. The name points at the rock, not at the gray powder in his dish. Glassmakers did not change their furnaces because a chemist had chosen a Latin root. They had been handling silicon's oxide all along, under shop names that never needed a periodic table.

trivia.title: Berzelius and the Gray Element
trivia.summary: An impure form of silicon already existed when Berzelius tried again. He wanted a sample clean enough to deserve the name he was about to publish.
trivia.story: Gay-Lussac and Thénard had prepared an impure silicon earlier, a hint rather than a settled element. In 1824 Jöns Jacob Berzelius reduced potassium fluorosilicate and obtained silicon that was reasonably pure. The product was not a gem and not a metal in the everyday sense. It was a gray, brittle element that chemistry could finally point to. Berzelius gave it the name from flint and put it on a firmer footing than the earlier dirty samples. Isolation, for silicon, meant separating it from the oxygen it loves, and the rocks had never given it up willingly.

trivia.title: The Earlier Dirty Sample
trivia.summary: Before Berzelius, two French chemists had already forced a silicon compound to yield something new. Their product was real enough to matter and too impure to settle the question.
trivia.story: Discovery is sometimes a second attempt that gets the credit because the first attempt was muddy. Gay-Lussac and Thénard reduced a silicon compound and obtained a substance that later knowledge recognizes as impure silicon. They did not yet have the clean element or the lasting account. The work sat in the background while Berzelius, in 1824, made the case that persuades a textbook. The earlier pair were not imagining things, and they were early. Silicon's history has this near-miss built into it: a dark, contaminated sample that pointed the right way and could not, by itself, finish the proof.

trivia.title: From Sand to the Chip
trivia.summary: For a century silicon was a chemical footnote beside its famous oxide, sand. Then electronics needed an element that could conduct a little, and not too much.
trivia.story: Silica remained the main way people met silicon: glass, stone, and mortar. The element itself was a poor conductor compared with copper and a poor insulator compared with glass, which looked like a useless middle, and twentieth-century electronics needed exactly that middle. Zone refining made silicon extraordinarily pure, and the transistor age, after an early start with another element, settled on silicon chips. A grain of purified sand, rearranged, became the engine of a calculator and then of almost every device in a pocket. The flint of the old name had become a wafer. The change was purity and design, not a new discovery of the element.

trivia.title: Dust That Scars the Lungs
trivia.summary: The oxide of silicon is ordinary in rock and in a workshop floor. Breathed as fine dust, year after year, it is not ordinary at all.
trivia.story: Quarry workers, miners, and stone cutters have always lived in dust, and not all dust is the same. Fine silica, the oxide that glass and flint are made of, can scar the lungs when it is inhaled for long enough. The disease is silicosis, a stiffening of the breath that no cough clears. It is not a sudden accident with a single bang. It is a slow injury from a substance that looks as harmless as sand on a beach, and silicon the element became the chip. Silica the dust remained a reason for masks, water sprays, and laws about the air in a cutting shed.

discovery.text: Found in Cornish ilmenite; Klaproth named it after the Titans.

elements.history:
William Gregor, a Cornish clergyman, found a new metal oxide in the black sand menachanite in 1791. Martin Heinrich Klaproth rediscovered it in a Hungarian ore in 1795 and named it titanium, for the Titans. Matthew Hunter isolated a pure ductile metal only in 1910.

The Kroll process of the 1940s made titanium a structural metal. Its oxide, already used as a white pigment, is still the form most people meet.
elements.howDiscovered:
William Gregor, in Cornwall, separated the black sand menachanite from the stream with a magnet, dissolved it in acid, and removed the iron. A white oxide remained. In 1791 he reported that the oxide was not a known earth. He did not obtain the metal.

Martin Heinrich Klaproth independently found the same oxide in Hungarian rutile in 1795 and gave the element its name. A ductile metal came only in 1910, when Matthew Hunter heated the chloride with sodium in a sealed bomb. The discovery was the white oxide that survived after the iron had been taken out of a magnetic sand.
elements.cosmicOrigin:
Stable titanium, mostly titanium-48, is a product of explosive silicon burning. The supernova assembles a radioactive parent, chromium-48, which decays through vanadium-48 down to titanium-48. The hot, expanding debris, called alpha-rich freeze-out, contributes more.

A radioactive cousin, titanium-44, is made in the same explosions and decays onward to calcium. Its gamma rays are still seen in the remnant Cassiopeia A. The titanium in an airframe is the stable isotope, frozen out of blasts of that kind before the Sun formed.

trivia.title: Black Sand in a Cornish Stream
trivia.summary: William Gregor was a clergyman who studied minerals in his spare hours. A black sand in his parish did not match the ores he knew.
trivia.story: In Cornwall, a black sand called menachanite collected in streams, heavy and easy to overlook. William Gregor, a clergyman with a chemist's habits, analyzed it in 1791 and found a new metal oxide mixed with iron. He suggested a new metal, sometimes remembered under a name drawn from the local valley. The report did not make him famous, and the oxide did not give up a useful lump of metal. Gregor had still seen the element first. Titanium's discovery begins with a parish curiosity and a careful amateur, not with a grand laboratory and a finished ingot.

trivia.title: Klaproth Names the Titans
trivia.summary: A few years after Gregor's sand, Martin Heinrich Klaproth met the same oxide in a different ore. He gave the metal a name large enough to stick.
trivia.story: Martin Heinrich Klaproth, working in 1795 on a Hungarian ore, rediscovered the oxide Gregor had found in Cornwall. He did not keep the local nickname. He named the metal titanium, for the Titans, the giant family of Greek myth. The name promised strength, which was optimistic, because nobody could yet isolate a clean, workable metal. Klaproth's authority as an analyst made the element real to other chemists in a way Gregor's parish paper had not, and two men had found one oxide. The mythological name won, and the Cornish sand became a footnote to a Titan.

trivia.title: A Century to a Workable Metal
trivia.summary: Knowing titanium's oxide was not the same as holding a bar that could be bent. The element stayed tangled with oxygen and nitrogen long after its name was settled.
trivia.story: Titanium's compounds were common enough, and the pure metal was exasperating. It soaks up oxygen and nitrogen when it is hot, so ordinary smelting produced a brittle mess rather than a ductile bar. Matthew Hunter finally isolated a pure, workable metal in 1910, more than a century after Gregor's sand, and the delay was the story, and chemists had not been lazy. The element had been difficult. Hunter's sample showed that titanium could be a metal in the practical sense, light and strong, once a workable sample finally existed. The Titans of the name had stayed stuck in their oxides for a century.

trivia.title: White Paint in the Can
trivia.summary: Most people never meet titanium metal. They meet the oxide, a fierce white pigment that replaced older whites with a dangerous reputation.
trivia.story: Titanium dioxide is brilliantly white, stable, and widespread in paint, plastic, and paper. For much of the twentieth century it pushed aside lead white, a pigment that had poisoned painters and residents for generations. The new white did the visual job without that particular metal's toxicity, and sunscreen and toothpaste later used the same oxide. A person can live among titanium compounds and never see the gray metal. Gregor's black sand and a bright kitchen wall are the same element, once as an ore and once as a pigment milled fine. The famous use is the color, not the structural bar.

trivia.title: The Kroll Process Arrives
trivia.summary: Hunter had proved that workable titanium existed. Industry still needed a route to tons of it, and that route came much later, in the middle of the twentieth century.
trivia.story: A laboratory ingot is a proof, and a factory is a different problem. In the 1940s William Kroll's process made titanium metal in industrial amounts rather than in pinches. Aircraft designers could order a light, corrosion-resistant metal instead of only admiring a laboratory lump. Titanium stopped being an oxide with a mythic name and became a structural metal beside aluminium and steel. The black sand Gregor found in Cornwall had taken about a hundred and fifty years to reach a factory floor.

applications.title: Classroom caution
applications.body: Element Deck describes published chemistry of Titanium. It is not a protocol for handling the element.
